data.title: An expedition to the Vikings 2013, part 1 – southern Sweden and Öland
data.excerpt: Ľubka of the Hradiská civic association travelled to Scandinavia in 2013 to get to know the history of the Vikings. In the first part she describes the 59-boulder stone ship of Ale je Stones at Kaseberga, the ancient fortress of Ismantorp borg on Öland, a runestone raised by the Danish leader Sibbe, the limestone alvar and the open-air museum at Eketorp.

children.text: Ľubka, a member of our Hradiská civic association, took part in an expedition to Scandinavia which was also devoted to getting to know the history of the Vikings. She has decided to share her experiences with us. Enjoy the reading.
Kaseberga

Our first stop on the way to knowledge is Kaseberga, at the megalithic national monument in southern Sweden — Ale je Stones.  
  On a rocky shelf above the sea, among grazing herds of cows, 59 large boulders rise, laid out in the shape of a ship. According to legend the legendary King Ale is buried here. Research suggests that the ship may have been created as much as 5500 years ago (the monoliths in the shape of a ship bear the name Ale stenar (Ale je Stones)), but most probably in AD 800–1050. Söderberg, the head of the archaeologists, claims that the stones are a kind of superstructure on original, far older ones. In the middle of the ship, at depth, they discovered the impressions of giant boulders removed long ago. They believe that this was a dolmen burial chamber.  
 
  Another legend says that the Viking leader who fell in the battle of Svolder is buried here.    
   The rocks were discovered under several metres of drifting sand in 1958, and the first archaeological excavations took place in 1989. Inside the ship a clay vessel was discovered. It contained bones dating from about 600 BC. They also discovered the remains of a hearth from this period.  The ship was built according to precise geometry (the cardinal points, months, days…)
Noahs ark

NOAHS ARK – stones laid out in the shape of a ship, apparently from about 3000 years ago, serving as a burial ground. So that the dead should have every comfort, their remains were laid in a ship and thus sent off to the other world. The dead were cremated and their ashes placed in a dug-out pit together with their valuables. Around the main ship, which is 26 m long, the archaeologists uncovered further graves of various sizes. The burial ground was in use until about the year 1500. In the surroundings there are several menhirs – tall upright flat stones. To this day nobody knows what they served for…
ISMANTORP BORG

ISMANTORP BORG is an ancient fortress in central Öland, 125 m in diameter, with 9 gateways, and at present it has 88 house foundations, the remains of a former village. In the middle of the fortification are the remains of a circular prehistoric square. The fortress served for about 600 years; it was built around the year 200.

What the fortress served for is a matter of guesswork only. For instance, were it not for a few weekend cottages in the Swedish style which spoilt the atmosphere of ages past for us, we felt as though we were in the Middle Ages. Despite its high, 4-metre walls, the fortress was probably weakly defended because of the number of its gateways. It may have served as a marketplace, but because of its thick and high walls all kinds of guesses circulate about its use.
Öland – a runestone

In Öland there is one of the oldest runestones in Sweden. It stands to the south of Kalmar. The stone lies among fields and was raised by the Danish leader Sibbe as a memorial to his son. The stone is 130 cm high, stands in its original place, and it was only at the beginning of the 17th century that burial mounds began to multiply in its surroundings.

The inscription, which it has been possible to decipher, reads “This stone was placed by Sibbi, the guardian, Foldar’s son, but his retinue was on the island.” It continues with verses which in translation read roughly HIDDEN KNOWS THAT THE GREATEST DEEDS ARE TO BE FOLLOWED. It is the only original verse that has survived on a runestone. Nothing more could be deciphered, and conjectures differ.
We photographed the stone, stroked it, and drew energy from it and from its message. Some of the women on the trip embraced it and let themselves be carried away by a breath of the otherworldly.
ALVAR

An alvar is a natural landscape of limestone pavement with a very thin layer of soil and poor vegetation, which can be used only as pasture. Kilometres of this “limestone paving” are to be found on Öland.

Far out on the steppe, some 8–10 km from civilisation or from any dwelling, stand two tall flat stones – menhirs. Nobody knows how they were raised, and so they have remained for whole generations. We needed a whole afternoon to reach the menhirs. We passed a herd of cows and crossed beautifully, colourfully flowering meadows, in places where conifers and a kind of dwarf pine were fighting for life.
It was a fine excursion and, after hours of sitting in the bus, it did us all good. The alvar is a steppe area included in a UNESCO protected area
Eketorp

We wanted to go to Eketorp straight to the place where life was once so busy. We arrived early – and so we filled the time until the open-air museum opened with a visit to the fishing village of Gräsgards Hamn. Circular defensive walls of enormous size greeted us, bathed in the morning sun. Here whole generations once lived together in a single community, worked, raised fearless and cruel warriors, and also died in the fighting for the fortress and for the territories they had already conquered.

It is fascinating to enter a kind of fortified village where you are welcomed by people in period costume, where you can step into workshops exactly like the original ones and make yourself, for example, an amulet cast from molten metal. You can then work it, hang it round your neck or take it home as a souvenir for your dearest.
Live piglets run about under our feet, we try archery, we plait a friendship bracelet – all of it with the expert assistance of “girls of blood and milk”.
In the little houses with straw (thatched) roofs people live, prepare food on the hearth, make love, simply live… at least that is what each of us imagines the moment we step inside the houses.

I go in to the master baker – he offers me a choice of flatbreads with various herbs. I choose the ordinary one – with caraway. I wait a little while for it to finish baking. It tastes excellent – I remember my childhood, when an old auntie used to bake flatbreads like this for us children as a treat, telling us at the same time her own stories from her poor but beautiful and happy childhood,…

Iveta and Martina became, for a while, opponents in a fierce fight to the death – period helmets on their heads, a mail shirt, swords even at their disposal, and they were already fighting. I come out of the fortification through a ruined stretch of the walls and find myself in front of a small vegetable garden fenced with the typical Y-shaped wooden fence, and a little way off a group of geese and ducks is swimming in a pond.

I return to the grounds of the open-air museum; our playful girls have found another amusement, a kind of tug-of-war, with which younger lads probably spent their free time in the past while toughening up their bodies. Among the houses I see a young man putting the byre and the fenced yard in order (I simply must have my photograph taken with him); what interests me most are his “krpce” – footwear made of leather strips joined together by a thin strap, also of leather. I go on, looking from one house into the next. The living quarters, a tiny hen house for the chickens, byres, areas for tools, hay under the roofs for the winter…

In fact everything that such a village needed is here. I can only marvel at how many superfluous things we need for life today, and how we chase after something we do not need at all – and perhaps we are not even living a full life… it gives one food for thought.

Peace, ease and admiration reign here, and suddenly I catch myself with the thought of spending some time here. In the company of these people, who bring the life of their ancestors close to us, and with the spirits that guard the fortification.
But time flies, and we must move on.
Ľubka J.
